analysis.one_liner: Requires states to draw congressional districts with independent commissions and bans mid-decade re-redistricting.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action: introduced May 11, 2023 with a single sponsor and zero cosponsors, it sat in the House Judiciary Committee until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would take the drawing of congressional district lines away from state legislators and hand it to independent commissions in every state. Commissions could not consider voters' party affiliation, voting history, or where incumbents live, and their meetings and maps would be posted publicly with software letting anyone draw and submit alternative maps. States would also be barred from redrawing congressional maps more than once per decade except when a court orders it, and federal grants of $150,000 per House seat would help pay for the commissions. It would take effect only for redistricting after the 2030 census.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters, especially in states where one party currently draws districts to protect its own seats. Voters would get districts drawn by a panel barred from considering party affiliation or incumbents' homes, with open meetings, published data, and a public tool for submitting their own maps. Communities would also gain from criteria prioritizing keeping counties, cities, and neighborhoods whole. Voters in states that redraw maps mid-decade for partisan gain would be protected by the once-per-decade limit.

how_it_helps.text: Every state must establish an independent redistricting commission to draw its congressional map, and commission members cannot have held public office, run for office, or worked for a party or candidate in the prior four years.
Commissions may not consider voting history, party affiliation, or the residence of incumbent House members when drawing districts, and must hold all meetings in public.

Each commission must maintain a public website with precinct-level census and voting data, interactive software any resident can use to draw a plan, and a channel for submitting proposed maps and comments.
A state may not be redistricted more than once after each decennial apportionment unless a court orders a new map to comply with the Constitution or the Voting Rights Act.
Districts must be drawn to keep counties, then municipalities, then neighborhoods together to the greatest extent practicable, and be compact and contiguous.

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent members of Congress and state legislative majorities would lose their power to draw the congressional maps that protect their seats, and political parties would lose a major tool for locking in House majorities. Taxpayers would fund the commissions through federal payments of $150,000 per House seat, which for a 435-member House totals roughly $65 million per decade.

drawbacks.text: The commissions are not fully independent of politicians: members are appointed by the majority and minority leaders of each chamber of the state legislature, so the two major parties still choose the mapmakers.
The bill takes effect only for redistricting after the 2030 census, so it would change nothing about the current maps for years.

If a commission's plan is not enacted, the state's highest court picks among commission-submitted plans without modification, and if the state fails to act, a federal district court draws the map — moving decisions to judges if the process stalls.

The strict ban on more than one redistricting per decade could delay legally needed fixes in a state unless a court orders the redraw, and the one-size-federal-template approach overrides states that already use their own methods.
The federal payments ($150,000 per Representative) are authorized with no dollar cap, an open-ended cost to taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — districts not drawn by the politicians they affect — addresses a widely felt problem, and the transparency requirements and once-per-decade limit are real checks. But the design has honest weaknesses: party legislative leaders still appoint every commissioner, the ban on mid-decade redraws could freeze in maps that later need legal correction, and it applies only after 2030. The taxpayer cost is modest in federal terms but uncapped. A supporter would fairly call the trade worthwhile; a skeptic would note that a commission chosen by the same legislative leaders it is meant to check is only partly independent.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee on May 11, 2023, and the committee never took it up; it died there when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the bill on May 11, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
No other member of the House — from either party — signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill received no committee markup, no vote, and no further action of any kind after its referral for the remainder of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent officeholders and legislative leaders keep their power to draw the congressional maps that protect their own seats, with no national rule changed before the next redistricting round after 2030.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote to measure a party split; the only support was one Democratic sponsor, and no member of either party cosponsored it.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and state legislators (incumbent officeholders)
industries.note: The bill strips politicians of the power to draw their own district lines and bans maps that consider incumbents' residences or voters' party affiliation. Incumbents' interest in keeping that power runs directly against voters' interest in fair districts.

Parties use map-drawing to lock in House seats and majorities; partisan gerrymandering would be barred, and commission appointees could not have worked for a party in the prior four years. Parties still pick the commissioners through legislative leaders, which softens the loss.
